content: Ensuring data integrity involves maintaining the consistency and accuracy of information, preventing any form of data corruption. Accountability is critical, meaning that individuals responsible for data collection must adhere to established principles and maintain confidentiality. Patients with tuberculosis (TB) should have access to their complete health records, whether in paper or electronic format. From an infection control perspective, transporting individuals with infectious TB should not occur until they have completed three months of treatment or are confirmed to no longer be infectious. Ground transport, such as ambulances or private vehicles, is preferred over air transport, even for short distances. All personnel involved must be fully informed. If non-recirculating ventilation is available, maximize outdoor air inflow from the vehicle’s cab, directing airflow over the patient and out through the rear window or exhaust fan. Physical isolation of the cab from the rest of the vehicle is ideal, with minimal or no other passengers. Patients should wear surgical masks covering their mouth and nose. Personnel should use particulate respirators and follow universal precautions, such as wearing gloves, disposing of materials in biohazard bags, and avoiding aerosol generation of mycobacteria. In emergency TB care and prevention, services are continuously updated as new tools, interventions, and evidence emerge. Innovations aim to enhance universal access to TB tools and socioeconomic development, supporting the achievement of End TB targets. Systematic screening for TB among at-risk populations, including close contacts of TB patients, people living with HIV, and those with other risk factors, is essential. Screening should be expanded during stabilized emergency phases to include previously treated TB patients, individuals exposed to silica, those with untreated fibrotic lesions, and populations in correctional facilities or affected by emergencies. WHO guidelines recommend systematic TB screening for specific groups, such as people living with HIV, household contacts, and individuals in high-prevalence settings. Screening tools include symptom checks, chest radiography, and molecular diagnostic tests. Rapid molecular diagnostics, such as Xpert MTB/RIF and Truenat, are essential for detecting TB and drug resistance. These tests are suitable for peripheral laboratories and provide results within hours. Additional diagnostic tools, such as lateral flow assays for TB antigens in urine, are also available for point-of-care use. Effective TB management relies on rapid diagnosis, drug resistance detection, and timely treatment initiation. This requires access to modern diagnostic methods, efficient referral systems, and adherence to biosafety principles. Laboratory services must be available from the onset of emergencies, with WHO-recommended molecular diagnostics used as initial tests. Access to radiological services and re-assessment of diagnostic capacities should be arranged as needed.
